question: Select the grammatically correct sentence.
option_1: The warrior was waiting for an right time to attack the lion hiding in a cave.
option_2: The warrior was waiting for the right time to attack the lion hiding in the cave.
option_3: An warrior was waiting for a right time to attack the lion hiding in the cave.
option_4: The warrior was waiting for a right time to attack an lion hiding in the cave.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The warrior was waiting for the right time to attack the lion hiding in the cave.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — the article "a/an" is chosen according to the sound that follows it, not the spelling: "a" is used before a word beginning with a consonant sound, and "an" before a word beginning with a vowel sound.

• In the given sentence, "right" begins with the consonant sound /r/, so it must be preceded by "a" (or, since a specific, already-understood time is meant, by the definite article "the"); and "lion" begins with the consonant sound /l/, so it must be preceded by "a", never "an".

• Option 2 correctly uses "the right time" and "the lion", both grammatically sound, making the sentence free of article errors.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "an right time" wrongly uses "an" before the consonant sound of "right"; it should be "the right time" or "a right time".

• Option 3 is incorrect because "An warrior" wrongly uses "an" before the consonant sound of "warrior"; it should be "A warrior" or "The warrior".

• Option 4 is incorrect because "an lion" wrongly uses "an" before the consonant sound of "lion"; it should be "a lion" or "the lion".

NOTE

• Remember: it is the sound, not the letter, that decides "a" vs "an" — e.g. "an hour" (silent h), "a university" (sound "yoo-").

• Common SSC traps: "a European", "an MBA", "a one-rupee coin", "an honest man".

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym for the underlined word in the given sentence.
The hot sun enervated the labourer to the extent that he collapsed.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. weaken.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Enervate" means to weaken someone physically, mentally, or morally; to drain of strength or vitality. (कमजोर करना)
◦ Example: The prolonged illness enervated him so much that he could barely walk.

• In the given sentence, the hot sun drained the labourer of his strength, causing him to collapse — this matches the meaning "weaken".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Alleviate (कम करना): To make (pain, suffering, or a problem) less severe — a different sense of easing something, not weakening a person.

• Option 3: Energise (ऊर्जा देना): To give vigour or energy to someone — this is actually the antonym of "enervate", a common SSC trap.

• Option 4: Elevate (ऊंचा उठाना): To raise to a higher position or level — unrelated to loss of strength.

NOTE

• "Enervate" is a classic confusable word — despite sounding energetic, it means the opposite of "energise". Do not confuse it with "innervate" (to supply with nerves).

• Other words meaning "to weaken": debilitate, enfeeble, sap, exhaust, deplete.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph
A. I would attach as many as four of them to a crosspiece, rotably arranged on a thin spindle, and transmit the motion of the same to a large disc and so derive considerable 'power'.
B. In my next attempt I seem to have acted under the first instinctive impulse which later dominated me – to harness the energies of nature to the service of man.
C. These creatures were remarkably efficient, for once they were started they had no sense to stop and continued whirling for hours and hours and the hotter it was the harder they worked.
D. I did this through the medium of May-bugs – or June-bugs as they are called in America – which were a veritable pest in that country and sometimes broke the branches of trees by the sheer weight of their bodies.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. BDAC.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence B is the opening/topic sentence — it introduces the writer's "next attempt", driven by the impulse "to harness the energies of nature to the service of man"; this sets up what device or creature will be used.

• Sentence D follows logically, explaining how — "I did this through the medium of May-bugs" — the pronoun "this" in D refers back to the attempt mentioned in B, and it introduces the creatures (May-bugs/June-bugs) that will be described further.

• Sentence A continues the description of the mechanism — "I would attach as many as four of them" — "them" clearly refers to the May-bugs introduced in D, describing how the writer harnessed their motion using a crosspiece and spindle.

• Sentence C concludes the paragraph, commenting on the result/quality of the mechanism — "These creatures were remarkably efficient" — summing up the performance of the May-bugs already attached to the device in A.

• Reading B–D–A–C together produces a smooth, logically connected paragraph: attempt → method (May-bugs) → mechanism (attaching them) → outcome (their efficiency).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (BACD) is incorrect because sentence A ("I would attach as many as four of them") is placed before D, even though "them" in A can only be understood after D introduces the May-bugs.

• Option 2 (ACBD) is incorrect because it opens with A, whose pronoun "them" has no antecedent yet, making the paragraph opening unclear.

• Option 4 (DACB) is incorrect because it places B (the topic-introducing sentence about the writer's impulse) at the end, after the method and mechanism have already been described, disrupting the logical flow.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always locate the topic/introductory sentence first (one that makes a general statement, without pronouns needing an antecedent) — here, sentence B.

• Track pronouns like "them", "this", "these" — they must always follow the noun they refer to, never precede it.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Visious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Vicious" — meaning cruel, savage, or deliberately harmful.
◦ Example: The dog gave a vicious growl before attacking.

• Spelling key: VI + CIOUS — note the "c" before "ious", not "s". The word "Visious" wrongly replaces the "c" with an "s".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Hoarse" — correctly spelt; means a rough, harsh-sounding voice.

• Option 2: "Imprint" — correctly spelt; means a mark impressed on a surface.

• Option 3: "Precious" — correctly spelt; means of great value.

NOTE

• Other "-cious" ending words commonly tested by SSC: gracious, spacious, malicious, suspicious, delicious, atrocious, ferocious — all use "cious", never "sious" or "shous".

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
To move or travel back and forth frequently
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Shuttle.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Shuttle" means to move or travel back and forth frequently between two places. (बार-बार आना-जाना)
◦ Example: A free bus shuttles between the airport and the city centre every hour.

• The word originates from the weaving shuttle, which moves rapidly back and forth across the loom, carrying the weft thread.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Grapple (जूझना): To struggle or grip firmly while fighting or dealing with a difficult problem.

• Option 3: Rupture (टूटना/फटना): A break or tear, especially of tissue or a relationship.

• Option 4: Foster (बढ़ावा देना): To encourage or promote the development of something, or to bring up a child that is not one's own.

NOTE

• Other one-word substitutes for repeated/back-and-forth motion: "oscillate" (to swing back and forth), "commute" (to travel regularly between home and work), "vacillate" (to waver between opinions).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
My complaint is that the gardener dozes off during work.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Praise.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Complaint" means an expression of dissatisfaction or annoyance about something. (शिकायत)
◦ Example: The residents filed a complaint about the noise.

• The antonym of "complaint" is "Praise", which means to express approval or admiration. (प्रशंसा)
◦ Example: The teacher praised the student for his hard work.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Challenge (चुनौती): A call to take part in a contest, or something that tests one's abilities — not opposite in meaning to complaint.

• Option 2: Carp (नुक्ताचीनी करना): To find fault or complain unreasonably about trivial matters — this is actually a synonym of "complaint", not its antonym, a common SSC trap.

• Option 4: Demur (आपत्ति करना): To raise objections or show reluctance — again close in meaning to "complaint", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Words synonymous with "complaint": grievance, carp, gripe, protest, objection, demur.

• Words meaning the opposite (praise): commend, compliment, laud, extol, applaud.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
You can always dependent on me.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. depend on me.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence requires a verb, not an adjective, after the modal "can" — "can" is always followed by the base form (V1) of the verb, so "dependent" (an adjective) must be replaced by the verb "depend".

• Rule — the verb "depend" always takes the preposition "on/upon": depend on/upon someone/something.

• Applying the rule, the correct segment is "depend on me".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "depend" is never followed by "over"; no such standard collocation exists.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "depend" does not take the preposition "for"; "for" is used with words like "wait for", "ask for", not "depend".

• Option 3 is incorrect because "depend" does not take the preposition "at"; "at" is used with words indicating a specific point, such as "arrive at", "look at".

NOTE

• After a modal verb (can, could, will, would, shall, should, may, might, must), always use the base form (V1) of the main verb — never an adjective or a gerund.

• Other verb + preposition pairs frequently tested: rely on, count on, insist on, depend upon, dependent on (as an adjective, e.g. "he is dependent on his parents").

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Willing to take risks and try new ideas.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Adventurous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Adventurous" means willing to take risks or try out new methods, ideas, or experiences. (साहसी)
◦ Example: She has always been adventurous, happy to try any new sport.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Resolute (दृढ़ निश्चयी): Firm and determined in purpose, not necessarily related to taking risks or trying new things.

• Option 2: Desperate (हताश): Feeling or showing a hopeless sense that a situation is impossible to deal with; driven by great need, not willingness to try new ideas.

• Option 4: Mythical (काल्पनिक): Relating to myth, or existing only in imagination — unrelated to risk-taking.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes: "audacious" (boldly daring), "venturesome" (inclined to take risks), "intrepid" (fearless and adventurous).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Exuberance
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Vibrancy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Exuberance" means the quality of being full of energy, high spirits, and enthusiasm. (उत्साह/जोश)
◦ Example: The children greeted the holidays with great exuberance.

• "Vibrancy" carries the same sense of energy, liveliness, and enthusiasm, making it the closest synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Laziness (आलस्य): Unwillingness to work or use energy — the near opposite of exuberance.

• Option 3: Sympathy (सहानुभूति): Feeling of pity or sorrow for someone else's misfortune — unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: Impartiality (निष्पक्षता): The quality of treating all sides equally, without bias — unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "exuberance": zest, ebullience, exhilaration, high spirits, enthusiasm.

• Related adjective form: "exuberant" (full of energy and enthusiasm).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
Rakesh will win the lottery.
option_1: The lottery is won by Rakesh.
option_2: The lottery will have won by Rakesh.
option_3: The lottery will be won by Rakesh.
option_4: The lottery was won by Rakesh.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The lottery will be won by Rakesh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Rakesh will win the lottery" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Future Tense.

• Rule — Simple Future Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + will/shall + V1 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + will/shall + be + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the lottery" becomes the subject; the modal "will" is retained and followed by "be"; the verb "win" becomes the past participle "won"; and "Rakesh" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: The lottery will be won by Rakesh.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "is won" is the passive of the Simple Present Tense, not the Simple Future.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "will have won" is the active Future Perfect form, not a valid passive construction of a Simple Future sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "was won" is the passive of the Simple Past Tense, not the Simple Future.

NOTE

• The passive of the Simple Future Tense always uses the structure "will/shall + be + V3" — never drop the "be".

• Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, must, should, would) also form their passive with "modal + be + V3", e.g. "The work must be finished by Rakesh.".

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A.Those verses are collectively known as the Bhagavadgita.
B.His hesitation before the battle against his family became the occasion for his friend and charioteer, Lord Krishna, to deliver a discourse on dharma.
C.Arjuna was one of the five Pandava brothers, who are the heroes of the Indian epic, the 'Mahabharata'.
D.He was the son of the god Indra and was famous for his archery.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. CDBA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence C is the topic-opening sentence — it introduces the subject, "Arjuna", by name for the first time, along with context (one of the five Pandava brothers, heroes of the 'Mahabharata').

• Sentence D follows naturally, continuing to describe Arjuna using the pronoun "He" — giving further background (son of Indra, famous for archery).

• Sentence B then narrates a specific event in Arjuna's life — "His hesitation before the battle" — the possessive pronoun "His" refers back to Arjuna already introduced in C and D — leading to Krishna's discourse.

• Sentence A concludes the paragraph, referring back with "Those verses" to the discourse on dharma mentioned in B, and naming it as the Bhagavadgita.

• Reading C–D–B–A together forms a clear, logical narrative: who Arjuna was → more about him → the key event (Krishna's discourse) → the naming of that discourse as the Bhagavadgita.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (DCBA) is incorrect because it opens with D, whose pronoun "He" has no antecedent yet, since Arjuna has not been named.

• Option 3 (ABDC) is incorrect because it opens with A, whose phrase "Those verses" refers to something (the discourse) not yet mentioned, making the opening incoherent.

• Option 4 (BADC) is incorrect because it opens with B, whose possessive pronoun "His" has no antecedent, and disrupts the chronological flow of the narrative.

NOTE

• Always identify the sentence that names the subject explicitly (here, "Arjuna" in C) as the likely opening sentence in a para-jumble.

• Watch for demonstrative references like "those verses", "this discourse" — they must follow, not precede, the noun they point to.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Statinary.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is either "Stationary" (not moving; fixed in one place) or "Stationery" (writing materials such as paper and pens), depending on the intended meaning — but "Statinary" is not a correctly spelt word in either sense.

• Spelling key: STATION + ARY/ERY — note the "o" after "stati", which is missing in "Statinary".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Entrance" — correctly spelt; means the act or place of entering.

• Option 2: "Brief" — correctly spelt; means short in duration, or a short summary.

• Option 3: "Thunder" — correctly spelt; means the loud noise accompanying lightning.

NOTE

• "Stationary" (adjective, not moving) and "Stationery" (noun, paper/writing materials) are a classic pair of confusable homophones frequently tested by SSC — remember: "stationEry" has an "e", like "envelope" or "paper".

• Other commonly confused pairs: "principal/principle", "complement/compliment", "desert/dessert".

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
Authorities denied his simple request.
option_1: His simple request has been denied by authorities.
option_2: His simple request is denied by authorities.
option_3: His simple request had been denied by authorities.
option_4: His simple request was denied by authorities.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. His simple request was denied by authorities.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Authorities denied his simple request" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "his simple request" becomes the subject; being singular, the auxiliary is "was"; the verb "denied" (V2) becomes the past participle "denied" (V3); and "authorities" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: His simple request was denied by authorities.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "has been denied" is the passive of the Present Perfect Tense, not the Simple Past.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "is denied" is the passive of the Simple Present Tense, not the Simple Past.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "had been denied" is the passive of the Past Perfect Tense, not the Simple Past.

NOTE

• The passive of Simple Past Tense always uses "was/were + V3", matching the number of the new subject (singular → was, plural → were).

• "Deny" is a regular verb; V2 and V3 are both "denied".

question:
Select the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank.
The details were _________ from one person to the other within no time.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. passed down.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "pass down" means to hand on or transmit (information, a possession, or a tradition) from one person to another. (एक से दूसरे तक पहुँचाना)
◦ Example: The recipe has been passed down from grandmother to mother to daughter.

• In the given sentence, the details were transmitted from one person to another very quickly, which matches the sense of "passed down".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Pass away (गुज़र जाना): A polite way of saying "to die" — completely unrelated to the given context.

• Option 2: Pass in: Not a standard/idiomatic English phrasal verb; it does not fit the sentence.

• Option 4: Pass out (बेहोश होना / उत्तीर्ण होना): To lose consciousness, or (informally) to graduate/complete a course — neither meaning fits the context of details being transmitted.

NOTE

• Other important "pass" phrasal verbs for SSC: pass off (to happen/occur in a particular way, or to pretend something is genuine), pass on (to transmit information, or a euphemism for "to die"), pass over (to ignore or disregard someone for promotion).

• Do not confuse "pass down" (transmit through generations/chain) with "pass on" (also used for transmitting information) — both can be close in meaning, but "pass down" specifically fits a chain from one person to another.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The room was very________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. quiet.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence requires an adjective describing the room — "quiet" means making little or no noise; calm and silent, which correctly completes the sentence "The room was very quiet."

• The intensifier "very" must be followed by an adjective, and among the given options only "quiet" functions as an adjective suitable for describing a room.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Quit" — a verb meaning to stop or leave; it cannot follow "very" and does not fit grammatically.

• Option 2: "Quilt" — a noun meaning a padded bed-cover; unrelated in meaning and cannot follow "very".

• Option 4: "Quite" — an adverb meaning "completely" or "fairly" (e.g. "quite good"); it cannot be used after "very" and does not describe the room by itself.

NOTE

• "Quiet", "quit", "quilt" and "quite" are commonly confused due to their similar spelling — always check the part of speech required by the sentence: an adjective is needed after "very ___" when describing a noun.

• "Quiet" (adjective/noun: silence) vs. "Quite" (adverb: to a certain extent) is one of the most frequently tested confusable pairs in SSC exams.

question:
Select the correct idiom to replace the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Harry always speaks his eye but he is not always very diplomatic!
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. speaks his mind.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to speak one's mind" means to say openly and honestly exactly what one thinks, even if it may upset or offend others. (बेझिझक अपनी राय व्यक्त करना)
◦ Example: She is known for speaking her mind, no matter who is in the room.

• The sentence contrasts this trait with "not always very diplomatic", which fits perfectly with someone who speaks bluntly/honestly — i.e., speaks his mind.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "speaks his tongue" — not a standard English idiom; the correct related idiom is "bite one's tongue" (to stop oneself from saying something), which has the opposite sense.

• Option 2: "reads his heart" — not a standard idiom; a related idiom is "wear one's heart on one's sleeve" (to show one's emotions openly), which is different in meaning.

• Option 4: "listens his ear" — grammatically and idiomatically incorrect; no such standard idiom exists in English.

NOTE

• Other idioms related to plain-speaking: "call a spade a spade" (to speak frankly and directly), "not mince words" (to speak bluntly without softening the message).

• Do not confuse "speak one's mind" (say what one thinks) with "make up one's mind" (decide) or "cross one's mind" (occur as a thought).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Pass the buck
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Blaming another person.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to pass the buck" means to shift the responsibility or blame for something onto someone else, avoiding it oneself. (दोष दूसरे पर डालना)
◦ Example: Instead of admitting his mistake, the manager tried to pass the buck to his junior staff.

• The idiom originates from poker, where a marker called a "buck" was passed to the next player to indicate whose turn it was to deal — later extended to mean passing on responsibility.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Providing essential services — unrelated to the idiom's meaning of shifting blame.

• Option 2: Trying to calm down — this is closer to the idiom "keep one's cool" or "calm the waters", not "pass the buck".

• Option 4: Saying something unpleasant — this does not capture the sense of avoiding responsibility conveyed by "pass the buck".

NOTE

• The phrase "the buck stops here" (popularised by US President Harry Truman) means the opposite — taking full responsibility rather than passing it on.

• Other idioms about blame/responsibility: "point the finger at" (to accuse someone), "throw someone under the bus" (to blame or betray someone to save oneself).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
The lizard's light brown skin acts as camouflage in the desert sand.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. reveal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Camouflage" means to disguise or hide something by making it resemble its surroundings, so as to make it indistinguishable. (छिपाना/भेस बदलना)
◦ Example: The soldiers used branches to camouflage their tanks.

• The antonym of "camouflage" is "reveal", meaning to make something visible or known; to uncover. (उजागर करना)
◦ Example: The curtains were drawn back to reveal the stage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Clothed (वस्त्र पहना हुआ): Wearing clothes; unrelated to the concept of hiding vs. exposing.

• Option 2: Mask (नकाब): A covering used to hide the face or disguise something — this is actually a near-synonym of "camouflage", not its antonym.

• Option 4: Vanishing (लुप्त होना): Disappearing from sight suddenly — this is closer in meaning to "camouflage" (becoming unseen) rather than its opposite.

NOTE

• Words synonymous with "camouflage": disguise, conceal, mask, cloak, screen.

• Words meaning the opposite (reveal): expose, uncover, unveil, disclose, exhibit.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined word in the given sentence.
We have always been told retaliation is not the key to resolving problems.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. revenge.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Retaliation" means the act of attacking or harming someone in return for an injury or wrong; revenge. (बदला)
◦ Example: The company faced retaliation from its rival after the price cut.

• The word "retaliation" is a noun form of the verb "retaliate" (to return like for like, especially an injury).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Outcome (परिणाम): The result or consequence of an action — unrelated to the idea of returning harm.

• Option 3: Realisation (एहसास): Awareness or understanding of something — unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: Pamper (लाड़ प्यार करना): To indulge someone with excessive care or attention — entirely unrelated, and even opposite in tone.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "retaliation": vengeance, reprisal, requital, counterattack.

• Related idiom: "an eye for an eye" — a phrase associated with the concept of retaliation/revenge.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A)There is a general belief that these medicines heal ailments safely.
B)The 'safe healing' is actually that which doesn't have any side effects.
C)Positive healing without any unwanted effect on the body drives the trend.
D)Herbal medicines are a new trend these days.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. DABC.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence D is the topic-opening sentence — it introduces the subject in general terms: "Herbal medicines are a new trend these days".

• Sentence A naturally follows, elaborating on this trend with the general belief associated with it — "There is a general belief that these medicines heal ailments safely" — the phrase "these medicines" refers back to the herbal medicines introduced in D.

• Sentence B builds on the idea of "safely" from A by defining what "safe healing" actually means — "The 'safe healing' is actually that which doesn't have any side effects".

• Sentence C concludes the paragraph by summarising why this trend is driven — "Positive healing without any unwanted effect on the body drives the trend" — directly echoing "no side effects" from B.

• Reading D–A–B–C together produces a clear, logically progressing paragraph: topic → general belief → definition of "safe" → concluding reason for the trend.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (ADCB) is incorrect because it opens with A, whose phrase "these medicines" has no antecedent yet, since herbal medicines have not been introduced.

• Option 2 (DACB) is incorrect because it places C before B, but C's concluding statement about "the trend" logically belongs after B has defined "safe healing", not before.

• Option 4 (ACDB) is incorrect because, like Option 1, it opens with A without first introducing "herbal medicines" in D, leaving "these medicines" without a clear reference.

NOTE

• As with all para-jumbles, first locate the sentence that introduces the subject in general terms without unresolved pronouns/references — here, sentence D.

• Track referencing phrases like "these medicines", "the trend" — they must appear only after the noun they refer to has already been mentioned.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The structure of human psyche, as postulated by Sigmund Freud, (1)____________ of the ego, the super ego, and the id. The ego forms the part of our conscious mind which we work with and are most (2)_______ of. The super ego forms our conscience in the form of the unconscious and works on the (3)__________ of social and cultural influences. The id represents our subconscious which contains all (4)_________ thoughts, desires, and dreams. Dreams work as a free pathway into the subconscious, which is an inaccessible zone in general. It can also contain (5)__________ scenes or images that apparently have no relation to anything related to the person.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. consists.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "consist of" means to be made up of or composed of certain parts, and is the standard collocation used when listing the components of a structure — here, "the structure... consists of the ego, the super ego, and the id."

• Grammatically, the subject "The structure of human psyche" is singular, so the singular verb form "consists" (not "consist") is required to agree with it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "desires" does not fit grammatically or contextually; the sentence needs a verb meaning "is composed of", not a noun/verb meaning "wants or wishes for".

• Option 2: "lacks" would mean the structure is missing the ego, super ego and id — which contradicts the passage, since these three ARE the components of the psyche according to Freud.

• Option 3: "grapples" means "struggles with", which does not make sense in the context of describing what the psyche's structure is made up of.

NOTE

• "Consist of" is always used in the active voice and is never used in the continuous/progressive tense (i.e., never "is consisting of").

• Related expressions: "comprise" (the whole comprises the parts, used without "of" in formal style — "the structure comprises the ego, the super ego and the id"), "be composed of", "be made up of".

It can also contain (5)__________ scenes or images that apparently have no relation to anything related to the person.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. aware.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence states that the ego "forms the part of our conscious mind which we work with and are most _____ of" — since the ego belongs to the conscious mind, we are most "aware" of it, i.e., we have conscious knowledge or perception of it.

• "Aware of" is the standard collocation meaning having knowledge or perception of a situation or fact, which fits logically with the idea of the "conscious" mind described in the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "afraid" — means feeling fear; it does not fit the context, which is about consciousness/awareness, not fear.

• Option 2: "dependent" — means relying on something; this does not logically connect to being "conscious" of the ego.

• Option 4: "resistant" — means opposing or fighting against something; this contradicts the idea of "working with" the conscious mind, which suggests familiarity rather than resistance.

NOTE

• "Aware of" vs "conscious of" are near-synonyms and often interchangeable in such contexts — both indicate perception or knowledge of something.

• Common collocations: "aware of a fact", "conscious of one's surroundings", "mindful of consequences".

It can also contain (5)__________ scenes or images that apparently have no relation to anything related to the person.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. basis.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "works on the basis of" means operates or functions according to a foundation or set of principles — here, the super ego "works on the basis of social and cultural influences", meaning these influences form its foundation.

• "Basis" is the standard noun used after "on the" to indicate the foundation or grounds on which something operates (e.g., "on the basis of evidence").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "love" does not fit; "works on the love of social and cultural influences" is not idiomatic or meaningful in this context.

• Option 2: "counter" does not collocate meaningfully with "works on the ___ of"; it would suggest opposition, which is not supported by the passage.

• Option 3: "understanding" — while it seems plausible, "works on the understanding of social and cultural influences" changes the intended meaning to "comprehension of", rather than "founded upon", which is less precise than "basis" in this structural description of the super ego.

NOTE

• The fixed phrase "on the basis of" is frequently tested in SSC cloze passages, meaning "according to" or "founded upon".

• Related phrases: "on grounds of", "in accordance with", "founded on".

It can also contain (5)__________ scenes or images that apparently have no relation to anything related to the person.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. repressed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Repressed" means held back, suppressed, or kept from conscious awareness, which is precisely the Freudian concept being described: the id, representing the subconscious, contains all the repressed thoughts, desires, and dreams that have been pushed out of conscious awareness.

• This matches Freud's psychoanalytic theory, in which the id is the reservoir of instinctual, often repressed, urges and desires.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "heavy" — describes weight or intensity, not the psychological process of suppression; it does not fit the Freudian context.

• Option 3: "legal" — relates to law, entirely unrelated to the psychological description of the subconscious.

• Option 4: "sanctioned" — means officially approved or permitted, which contradicts the idea of hidden/suppressed thoughts in the subconscious.

NOTE

• "Repress" (verb) / "repression" (noun) / "repressed" (adjective) are key terms in Freudian psychology, referring to the unconscious exclusion of painful or unacceptable thoughts, memories, and desires from awareness.

• Related psychological terms: "suppression" (conscious, deliberate holding back, as opposed to "repression" which is unconscious), "subconscious", "id/ego/super ego".

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. bizarre.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Bizarre" means very strange or unusual, especially in a striking or unsettling way — fitting the description of dream scenes or images that "apparently have no relation to anything related to the person", since such unrelated, strange imagery is aptly called "bizarre".

• The passage describes dreams as containing scenes that seem to make no logical sense in relation to the dreamer's life — this unusual, seemingly random quality is best captured by "bizarre".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "parallel" — means running alongside or corresponding to something; this contradicts the idea of images having "no relation" to the person.

• Option 2: "constricted" — means narrowed or restricted; this does not describe the nature of dream imagery discussed here.

• Option 3: "concurrent" — means happening at the same time; this is unrelated to the described quality of dream scenes being unconnected to the person.

NOTE

• "Bizarre" is commonly used to describe dreams, events, or behaviour that is strikingly odd or inexplicable.

• Synonyms of "bizarre": strange, surreal, peculiar, outlandish, weird.
